$$
{\int }_{1}^{3}c\cdot f(t)\,\text{d}t=c\cdot {\int }_{1}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t.

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{3}c\cdot f(t)\,\text{d}t & =c\cdot {\int }_{1}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(4\,i-j+u\,k)\cdot (\frac{e}{2}\,i+3e\,j-k) \\  & =2e-3e-u \\  & =-e-u.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${\int }_{1}^{3}c\cdot f(t)\,\text{d}t=0,$ we must have $-e-u=0,$ which means that $u=-e.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Applying the Vector Addition and Scalar Multiplication Rules
canonical_examples.problem: Calculate $\displaystyle{\int_0^2} [  3 \mathbf f(t)+\mathbf g(t) ] \,\textrm{d}t$ given that $\displaystyle{\int_0^2} \mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t=\left\langle 16, \: 2,\: -2\right\rangle$ and $\displaystyle{\int_0^2}\mathbf g(t)\,\textrm{d}t=\left\langle 2,-4,2\right\rangle .$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
From the vector addition and scalar multiplication rules, we have

$$
\displaystyle {\int_0^2 } \big[ \, 3 \mathbf f(t)+\mathbf g(t) \, \big] \, \textrm d t =  \displaystyle {3\int_0^2 } \mathbf f(t) \, \textrm d t + \displaystyle {\int_0^2 } \mathbf g(t) \, \textrm d t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}[3f(t)+g(t)]\,\text{d}t & =3{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{2}g(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =3⟨16,\,2,\,-2⟩+⟨2,\,-4,\,2⟩ \\  & =⟨48,\,6,\,-6⟩+⟨2,\,-4,\,2⟩ \\  & =⟨50,2,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Reversing the Limits of Integration
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t & =-{\int }_{2}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-⟨-3,\,2,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨3,\,-2,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the vector addition rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)+⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{2}⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨3,\,-2,\,-1⟩+⟨t,\,-t,\,t⟩{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =⟨3,\,-2,\,-1⟩+⟨2,\,-2,\,2⟩\text{ } \\  & =⟨5,\,-4,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Applying the Adjacent Intervals Rule
canonical_examples.problem:
Calculate 
$\displaystyle\int_{-1}^0\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t$
given that
$\displaystyle\int_0^1\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t= \left\langle \dfrac{3}{2}, \: 1, \: 3 \right\rangle$
and
$\displaystyle\int_{-1}^1\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t=\left\langle 0, \: 2, \: 6 \right\rangle.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Using the adjacent intervals, we get

$$
\int_{-1}^1\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t=\int_{-1}^0\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t+\int_0^1\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t .
$$

We can rearrange the above as follows:

$$
\int_{-1}^0\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t = 
\int_{-1}^1\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t - \int_0^1\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t
$$

Finally, using the given information, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨0,\,2,\,6⟩-⟨\frac{3}{2},\,1,\,3⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{3}{2},\,1,\,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Applying the Product Rules
canonical_examples.problem:
Find $\displaystyle {\int_0^1 }  \mathbf c \times \mathbf f(t)  \, \textrm d t$ 
given that 
$\displaystyle\int_0^1\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm d t = \mathbf i-3\,\mathbf j-4\,\mathbf k$ 
and 
$\mathbf c=\mathbf j-\mathbf k .$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The cross-product rule states that

$$
{\int_0^1 } \mathbf c \times \mathbf f(t) \, \textrm d t =  \mathbf c \times {\int_0^1 } \mathbf f(t) \, \textrm d t  .
$$

 

Applying the cross-product rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t & =c\times {\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(j-k)\times (i-3\,j-4\,k) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -3 & -4\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}|k \\  & =(-4-3)i-(0+1)j+(0-1)k \\  & =-7\,i-\,j-\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Since the integration of vector functions is done component-by-component, the properties of integrals of vector functions are immediately inherited from those of the integrals of real-valued functions. 

Suppose that $\mathbf f(t)$ and $\mathbf g(t)$ are vector-valued functions that are continuous on a closed interval $[a,b],$ and $\alpha$ is a scalar. 
Then, the *vector addition and scalar multiplication rules* are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{a}^{b}(f(t)+g(t))\text{d}t={\int }_{a}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t\,+\,{\int }_{a}^{b}g(t)\,\text{d}t\, & \text{vector addition rule} \\ {\int }_{a}^{b}\alpha \,f(t)\,\text{d}t=\alpha \,{\int }_{a}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t\, & \text{scalar constant multiple rule}\end{aligned}
$$

  

For example, if $\mathbf f(t) = \left\langle t, \: \cos t\right\rangle$ and $\mathbf g(t) = \left\langle -t^2, \: \sin t \right\rangle,$ then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int [f(t)+2g(t)]\text{d}t & =\int f(t)\,\text{d}t+2\int g(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t+2\int ⟨-{t}^{2},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int t\,\text{d}t,\,\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩+⟨2\int -{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t,\,2\int \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{C}_{2}⟩+⟨-\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3}+{C}_{3},\,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{C}_{4}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3{t}^{2}-4{t}^{3}}{6},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

  

where $C_1, \, C_2, \, C_3, \, C_4$ are arbitrary real constants and ${\mathbf C} = \langle C_1+C_3, C_2+C_4 \rangle$ is a constant vector.

tutorials.name: The Rule for Reversal of Integration Limits
tutorials.problem:
Given a vector-valued function $\mathbf f(t)$ that is continuous on a closed interval $[a,b],$ the *rule for reversal of integration limits* states the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{b}^{a}f(t)\,\text{d}t=-{\int }_{a}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{a}^{b}[c\cdot f(t)]\text{d}t=c\cdot ({\int }_{a}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t)\, & \text{dot product rule} \\ {\int }_{a}^{b}[c\times f(t)]\text{d}t=c\times {\int }_{a}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t\, & \text{cross product rule}\end{aligned}
$$
